implementation_notes: The runtime mechanism is JavaScript's revocable proxy, so the forwarder and the revoker are still the { proxy, revoke } pair returned by Proxy.revocable; what TypeScript adds is the type discipline: declare the contract as an interface, build the proxy against it and expose only that interface, so callers cannot see the raw target. Interfaces are erased at runtime and mediate nothing, so the check stays in the handler traps and the failure surfaces as the runtime TypeError (or as an error you throw yourself in the trap). Choose an explicit Result-returning facade when callers must handle revocation in the type rather than in a catch block.
pitfalls: The interface is compile-time only: `as Session` performs no check, and any code path that still holds the target keeps full access - the type does not make the revocation complete.

A revoked proxy throws TypeError from the traps, which is not part of the interface's declared behaviour; either document the throw or wrap the trap and throw a modelled error (or return a Result) so callers can handle it deliberately.

Structural typing means the target itself satisfies the interface, so passing the target where Session is expected type-checks; a reviewer cannot see from the type that the raw object leaked out of the grant.
